title: Term 1 and 2 Examination
instructions: This paper covers the work of Terms 1 and 2.
This question paper consists of 6 questions. Answer ALL the questions.
Read each question carefully before you answer it.
Show your working, and round your answers as each question asks.

sections.title: QUESTION 1: Reading for Comprehension
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: Practice passage: The Water Tank (original text written for FreeSheet)
context.text:
When the taps in Mamelodi ran dry for the third week, Thando's grandmother did something nobody expected. She sold her old sewing machine.

With the money, and with help from three neighbours, she bought a second-hand plastic water tank and two lengths of gutter. On Saturday morning half the street gathered to watch the men fix the gutters to the roof. 'You will see,' Gogo said, though there had not been a cloud for a month. 'The rain always comes back to those who are ready for it.'

The rain came eleven days later, heavy and sudden, drumming on the tin roof. By morning the tank was full. Gogo hung a small sign on the gate: WATER FOR COOKING AND DRINKING. TAKE ONE BUCKET. LEAVE A SMILE.

By December, four more houses on the street had tanks of their own.

questions.prompt: A question that asks you to read between the lines is…
How many days later did the rain come, according to the passage?
Explain why the writer uses the word 'drumming' to describe the rain.
questions.memo:
✓ It suggests the loud, steady, rhythmic sound of heavy rain on the tin roof (1)
✓ It creates a vivid / joyful mood after the long drought (1)

questions.prompt: According to the passage, it was raining on the Saturday the gutters were installed.
questions.explanation: 'There had not been a cloud for a month.'

questions.prompt: Match each question to its level.

sections.title: QUESTION 3: Narrative and Descriptive Essays
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: Example paragraph: The market at dawn (original)
context.text: The market wakes before the sun. Gas burners hiss into life beneath dented pots, and the smell of frying vetkoek drifts between the stalls like a lazy cat. A vendor slaps a crate of tomatoes onto her table, each one as red and shiny as a fire engine. Somewhere a radio crackles with morning news, competing with the rattle of a trolley over uneven paving stones. My fingers, still cold, wrap gratefully around a paper cup of sweet, milky tea.

questions.prompt: The main purpose of a narrative essay is to…

sections.title: QUESTION 4: Poetry and Figures of Speech
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: Grandfather's Hands (an original poem written for FreeSheet)
context.text:
My grandfather's hands are maps of old roads,
cracked rivers running from knuckle to wrist.
They have carried bricks and babies,
held the reins of stubborn donkeys,
and once, a lifetime ago, a girl's shy hand
at a wedding in the rain.

Now they rest on the arms of his chair
like two tired birds after a long migration.
But when the radio plays the old songs,
they wake, they tap, they drum, drum, drum
the beat of every year he has danced through.

questions.prompt: 'The old car groaned up the hill.' This is an example of…
What is a word that sounds like the noise it describes called?
What is a group of lines in a poem called?
In 'Grandfather's Hands', identify the sound device in 'they drum, drum, drum' and explain its effect.
questions.memo:
✓ Repetition / onomatopoeia (1)
✓ It imitates the rhythm of his tapping to the music and shows his joy and energy returning (1)

questions.prompt: What is the theme of the poem?
questions.memo: ✓✓ e.g. Old age does not erase a person's rich life and spirit; the body may tire but memories and joy remain (2)

questions.prompt: 'Grandfather's Hands' follows a regular rhyme scheme.
questions.explanation: It is written in free verse.

sections.title: QUESTION 6: Friendly and Formal Letters
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: Example friendly letter (original)
context.text:
14 Jacaranda Street
Polokwane
0699
12 May 2025

Dear Lerato,

Thank you so much for the book you sent for my birthday! I started reading it on the bus and nearly missed my stop.

Guess what? Our soccer team made it to the district final. Coach says we have a real chance if our goalkeeper stops letting in silly goals (that's me, by the way).

How is life in Cape Town? Is it true that the wind blows people off the pavement? Write back soon and tell me everything.

Love,
Karabo

questions.prompt: If you begin with 'Dear Sir/Madam', how should you end a formal letter?
If you begin 'Dear Mr Dlamini', which closing should you use? (two words)
A friendly letter needs a subject line.
Which address is included in a formal letter but NOT in a friendly letter?
Give THREE features that show the letter to Lerato is informal.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): only the sender's address; 'Dear Lerato' first name; chatty tone; exclamations; contractions (that's); humour; 'Love,' ending; no subject line
